implementation_notes: Swift's concurrency runtime exposes the buffering decision in the initialiser: AsyncStream(bufferingPolicy:) takes .bufferingNewest(n) (keep the newest and discard older buffered elements), .bufferingOldest(n) (refuse newcomers once the bound is reached) or .unbounded, and the continuation's yield is what the policy applies to - so the bound is declared where the stream is created rather than in the consumer. Because the standard library strategy covers only the two drop policies, a blocking/back-pressure choice is expressed with an actor-held queue or by not yielding faster than the consumer; a bounded policy plus an explicit drop counter is the honest form of this pattern in Swift. Where the producer is a slow subscriber chain rather than an async sequence, the equivalent knob is Combine's buffering.
pitfalls: .unbounded is the policy of several convenience APIs: a hot producer with a slow consumer then grows without limit, so the bound must be stated explicitly.
Drops are invisible to the consumer - track produced-versus-consumed counts in the producing closure, or the loss only surfaces as missing data later.
A suspended consumer applies no pressure to an unbounded buffer; the policy, not the stream, is the bound.

variants.name: Combine buffer(size:prefetch:whenFull:)
variants.implementation_notes: Combine states the same decision as a pipeline operator: buffer(size:prefetch:whenFull:) collects up to size elements from upstream and applies the declared action when the buffer is full - dropOldest keeps the newest, dropNewest discards newcomers, dropWhileFull discards everything arriving while the buffer is full (a 'latest state' style policy). The decision is therefore written once, at the edge of the pipeline, instead of inside a custom queue. Choose it when the surrounding code is Combine-based; when the flow is async/await, the standard-library AsyncStream policy or an async queue is the better fit, and a stalled sink downstream of buffer() still needs its own timeout or counter.
pitfalls: dropOldest, dropNewest and dropWhileFull lose different data (oldest / newest / everything during the full period): the choice is semantic, not a performance knob.
buffer() upstream of a slow sink hides consumer stalls - pair it with a timeout or a drop counter, otherwise the first evidence is missing data.
Combine subscriptions must be retained: a cancelled or deallocated subscription silently ends the flow, which looks like a 'dropped everything' policy.
